title: Nicholas of Myra
hook: a bishop who, the story goes, dropped gold through a poor family's window by night

segments.voice: Yesterday, Athanasius, and your line was against the world. Did the truth you named come up, and did you say it kindly? Day seven hundred seventy.

A bag lands on the floor in the dark. It came through the window. Inside, there's gold. That's the scene at the heart of today's story, and it's an old one. A bishop named Nicholas, in Myra, a town near the southern coast of what's now Turkey. The red coat, the sleigh and the reindeer come much later, and from somewhere else entirely. Before any of that, there's a family in trouble, a window, and a man who very much didn't want to be thanked. We know little about Nicholas from records of his own time. What we have is mostly the story people told about him, again and again, and the way his church remembered him.

Here's how the old Lives of Nicholas tell it. A man in Nicholas's town had been well off and lost everything. He had three daughters, and no money for their dowries, which meant no marriages. The story says he was close to a terrible choice: letting his daughters be sold into shame to keep the household alive. Nicholas heard. He didn't knock on the door. He didn't call a meeting or make a speech. At night, he went to the house and threw a bag of gold in through the window, and left. The father woke up, found it, and wept, and the first daughter was married. Nicholas came back, another night, and did it again. And on the third night, the father was waiting. He ran after the shadow in the street, caught up, and fell at his feet. And what does Nicholas do? He begs the man to tell no one. That's the center of the story. Not the gold, the secret. It sounds like a page out of Jesus' teaching in Matthew's Gospel: "when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth: That thine alms may be in secret." As the story tells it, Nicholas didn't want the father to owe him, or to feel watched, or to have to be grateful in public. He wanted three young women to be safe and a father to keep his dignity. Orthodox and Catholic Christians honor him as a saint, and in some places children still find gifts on his feast. Whatever the history behind it, the shape the story keeps is this: help that arrives in the dark, with no name on it.

Here's the practice: settle, and breathe. Think of someone who could use help and wouldn't like to ask for it. A neighbor, a coworker, a student, a relative quietly having a hard month. Let one person come. Now think of one gift you could give them without your name on it. Groceries left on a step. A bill paid. A gift card in an unmarked envelope. A good word about them said to someone else, when they're not there. Pick one, small enough to actually do. Then picture yourself walking away before anyone sees. If you pray, you can pray for them. The bell holds the time.
Nicholas. A bishop near the southern coast of what's now Turkey who, the story goes, threw gold through a poor family's window by night, and begged not to be thanked.

Your line: a gift by night. This week: nurses in a plague, a man walking into the desert, an emperor, a letter, a word, an exile, and a bag through a window. Today, give your secret gift, and tell no one. Day seven hundred seventy.

Editor pass: Myra is described as 'near' rather than 'on' the southern coast (the ancient town lay a little inland). In the traditional Lives the dowry story may be set in Patara, Nicholas's hometown, before he was bishop; the teach says only 'a man in Nicholas's town'. Confirm.

Second editor pass: cut the hook's closing 'Today: the story.' (the same 'Today: ...' closer ran through several nearby hooks), and framed Nicholas's motives ('didn't want the father to owe him...') as 'as the story tells it', since they are the narrator's reading of the Life.
